expectedText:
INVENTION ASSIGNMENT & CONFIDENTIALITY AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

OWNERSHIP OF WORK PRODUCT
Work Jordan Lee creates for Acme, Inc. within the scope of employment is generally owned by Acme, Inc. from the moment it's created — this is the “work made for hire” doctrine. That default applies to work actually created within an employment relationship as the law defines it, not just work created by someone Acme, Inc. calls an employee. Courts look at factors like who controls how the work gets done, who provides the tools and workspace, how the work is paid for, and whether the person receives employee benefits and is treated as an employee for tax purposes — no single factor decides it on its own. Work created outside that scope, or by a contractor rather than an employee, is not automatically owned by Acme, Inc. under this doctrine.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "A “work made for hire” is— (1) a work prepared by an employee within the scope of his or her employment; or (2) a work specially ordered or commissioned for use as a contribution to a collective work, as a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, as a translation, as a supplementary work, as a compilation, as an instructional text, as a test, as answer material for a test, or as an atlas, if the parties expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them that the work shall be considered a work made for hire."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 101 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, definition of “work made for hire” (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/101)
  "In the case of a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author for purposes of this title, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 201(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, ownership of work made for hire (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/201)
  "In determining whether a hired party is an employee under the general common law of agency, we consider the hiring party's right to control the manner and means by which the product is accomplished."
  — Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730 (1989) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/112273/community-for-creative-non-violence-v-reid/)
  "Some factors, therefore, will often have little or no significance in determining whether a party is an independent contractor or an employee. In contrast, there are some factors that will be significant in virtually every situation. These include: (1) the hiring party's right to control the manner and means of creation; (2) the skill required; (3) the provision of employee benefits; (4) the tax treatment of the hired party; and (5) whether the hiring party has the right to assign additional projects to the hired party. These factors will almost always be relevant and should be given more weight in the analysis, because they will usually be highly probative of the true nature of the employment relationship."
  — Aymes v. Bonelli, 980 F.2d 857 (2d Cir. 1992) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/596113/clifford-scott-aymes-v-jonathan-bonelli-doing-business-as-island-swimming/)
  Known gap: This clause describes the employee branch of the work-made-for-hire doctrine only. Work by a contractor or consultant is “made for hire” only if it falls into one of nine narrow categories listed in 17 U.S.C. §101 (things like a contribution to a collective work, a translation, an instructional text) and the parties sign a written agreement saying so — most contractor work doesn't qualify, and needs a separate written assignment to transfer ownership at all. That separate-assignment situation isn't covered by this clause. One more precision point: §101 only defines the term “work made for hire” — the provision that actually vests ownership in the employer is 17 U.S.C. §201(b), which also contains its own carve-out: ownership vests in the employer “unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them.” That carve-out is exactly why a written assignment agreement like this one still matters even for work that already qualifies as made for hire — it isn't a redundant formality.

IF THIS IS SIGNED AFTER EMPLOYMENT BEGINS
If this agreement is signed after Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. has already started, rather than at hiring, some states require something of value beyond continued employment for the agreement to be enforceable — and courts around the country don't agree on this. Some courts have held that continuing to employ an at-will employee is itself enough to support an assignment or noncompete agreement signed later. Other courts have held the opposite: that continued at-will employment alone isn't enough, and something further — a raise, a bonus, a new role — is needed for the later agreement to be enforceable. Which rule applies depends on the state whose law governs this agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "We conclude that forbearance on the part of an at-will employer from discharging an at-will employee serves as consideration to support a noncompetition agreement."
  — Lake Land Employment Group of Akron, LLC v. Columber, 101 Ohio St. 3d 242 (2004) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/6892723/lake-land-employment-group-of-akron-llc-v-columber/)
  "A noncompete agreement entered into after employment has commenced is validly formed only when there is independent consideration at the time the agreement is reached. Finding that there was no independent consideration at the time of the 2002 noncompete agreement, we reverse the trial court's summary judgment ruling."
  — Labriola v. Pollard Group, Inc., 100 P.3d 791 (Wash. 2004) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2634466/labriola-v-pollard-group-inc/)
  Known gap: This document doesn't collect a governing-state field, so which side of this split applies can't be resolved automatically here. Courts have gone both ways on this exact question, and which rule applies depends on the state whose law governs this agreement. One more thing worth naming: both cited cases are noncompete cases, not invention-assignment or confidentiality cases. Their reasoning leans on public policy specific to noncompetes — courts have historically treated restraints on trade with "skepticism," a concern that doesn't apply the same way to an agreement that doesn't restrict where someone can work afterward. Whether courts would apply the identical consideration rule to an invention-assignment or confidentiality agreement specifically wasn't found in this research — this clause applies the noncompete-consideration rule by analogy, not because a court has confirmed it extends this far.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate your agreement to the terms above.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________

—
